title: Agentic AI versus pediatric emergency physicians for differential diagnosis of acutely ill and injured children
authors: Georgette, N.; Buckley, T.; Fine, A. M.; Jones, J.; McMurry, A. J.; Geanacopoulos, A.; Genadry, K. C.; Hoffmann, R.; Kahane, C.; Manrai, A. K.; Mandl, K. D.
abstract: BackgroundMisdiagnosis and delayed diagnosis of children in pediatric emergency departments lead to complications, and are particularly problematic in settings with limited pediatric expertise. Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in diagnostic reasoning for adult emergency department patients, but utility for pediatric cases is largely untested. MethodsRetrospective study of patients seen in the emergency department of a major urban pediatric academic medical center and subsequently admitted to the operating room or inpatient service. Records from 100 patients were randomly selected, stratified by age. We compared the accuracy of differential diagnoses (up to five, ranked by likelihood) generated by a previously developed agentic AI system, Dr. CaBot (one configuration with literature search, the other without), with those of four attending pediatric emergency medicine physicians (diagnosticians), all masked to outcome. Encounters were presented to diagnosticians stepwise across four touchpoints: triage, the initial physician evaluation (the a priori primary touchpoint), the full emergency department encounter, and the admission. Ground truth diagnosis was determined by two independent, board-certified pediatric emergency physicians (reviewers) based on the entire clinical encounter. The reviewers, masked to source, then assigned each differential a Bond score (0 to 5; 4 or above was high-scoring). FindingsThe median patient age was 4 years and 41% had a complex chronic condition. Bond score agreement between the two physician reviewers had a weighted kappa of 0.64. For the primary comparison at the initial physician evaluation touchpoint, Dr. CaBot and the diagnosticians both achieved high-scoring differentials in 95% of cases (difference 0%, 95%CI: -5.8, 5.8%). No differences were detected at the other touchpoints. InterpretationDr. CaBot and attending pediatric emergency medicine physicians showed similar performance in generating differential diagnoses from clinical documentation, suggesting potential as a diagnostic aid. Whether this performance can be translated into improvements in care requires prospective evaluation. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed using the query ((Pediatric[Title/Abstract]) AND (Emergency medicine[Title/Abstract]) AND ((Artificial Intelligence[Title/Abstract]) OR (Diagnostic reasoning[Title/Abstract]))), for articles published from 1 January 2000 to 31 December 2025, yielding 28 results, of which 16 were deemed not relevant based on title, 6 were reviews not presenting novel data, and 3 were surveys of physician perspectives on artificial intelligence (AI). There were 3 remaining studies of AI applications to pediatric emergency populations. One assessed AI management decisions of critically ill patients. One attempted to automate triage categorization using machine learning. One assessed the diagnostic reasoning of various general large language models (LLMs; e.g. ChatGPT-4o) on adapted cases from a pediatric emergency department in Italy. Overall, there is limited data on the use of specialized AI agents on diagnostic reasoning on real-world pediatric emergency cases. Added value of this studyThe diagnostic accuracy of an LLM-based agentic process was similar to that of four attending pediatric emergency medicine physicians across 100 cases of children evaluated in a pediatric emergency department. Using real world data from electronic health records and a masked multi-physician evaluation of open-ended agentic responses, we demonstrated physician-level accuracy of artificial intelligence in generating differential diagnoses for children. Implications of all the available evidenceThe agent shows promise as a diagnostic aid among children presenting to the emergency department.

infographic.key_insight: At initial physician evaluation, Dr. CaBot and pediatric emergency physicians each generated high-scoring differential diagnoses in 95% of cases.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Agentic AI may support pediatric emergency diagnostic reasoning, but improved patient care has not been demonstrated.
method: Retrospective study of 100 age-stratified, randomly selected pediatric emergency patients subsequently admitted to surgery or inpatient care.
Compared Dr. CaBot, with and without literature search, against four attending pediatric emergency physicians across four documentation touchpoints.
Two independent physician reviewers scored ranked differentials of up to five diagnoses, masked to their source.
infographic.evidence_signal: At the primary touchpoint, the difference in high-scoring differentials was 0 percentage points (95% CI: −5.8 to 5.8); reviewer agreement had a weighted kappa of 0.64.
infographic.watch_item: This single-center, retrospective evaluation of admitted patients requires prospective validation before conclusions about real-world safety or patient benefit.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic AI versus pediatric emergency physicians for differential diagnosis of acutely ill and injured children

title: OmniTongue: A Comprehensive MLLM Benchmark for Automated Tongue Diagnosis in Traditional Chinese Medicine
authors: Liuyi Xu, Yun Guo, Shusheng Li, Xuewen Zhang, Yining Qian, An-Yang Lu
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have excelled in Western medical imaging, yet their potential in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) tongue diagnosis remains systematically unevaluated. Tongue diagnosis requires sophisticated global and local perception, serving as a rigorous touchstone for assessing the visual understanding depth of MLLMs. However, existing datasets are limited by single dimensions, coarse granularity, and ambiguous labels, hindering the evaluation of authentic clinical capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce OmniTongue, the first comprehensive, fine-grained Visual Question Answering benchmark for TCM tongue diagnosis. This benchmark integrates 1,351 expert-validated images and 21,616 instruction pairs. Its core design features 16 clinical dimensions for multidimensional evaluation, region-specific annotations for pathological localization, and 66 fine-grained labels for precise diagnostic representation. Extensive evaluations of existing MLLMs reveal significant performance gaps, demonstrating that medical-specific models lack domain advantages, while universally poor Macro-F1 scores expose a reliance on statistical shortcuts rather than genuine understanding of tongue pathology. These findings not only highlight the current limitations of MLLMs in interpreting regional medical features but also underscore OmniTongue's significance for developing robust automated tongue diagnosis models. The code and dataset will be made publicly available in a future release.

infographic.key_insight: OmniTongue reveals substantial gaps in MLLMs’ ability to interpret fine-grained tongue features in Traditional Chinese Medicine, with no clear advantage for medical-specific models.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The benchmark supports research into automated TCM tongue assessment but does not establish clinical diagnostic validity or readiness.
method: Constructed a visual question answering benchmark from expert-validated tongue images.
Annotated 16 clinical dimensions, regional features, and 66 fine-grained labels.
Evaluated existing MLLMs on detailed tongue-feature interpretation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The benchmark includes 1,351 images and 21,616 instruction pairs; universally poor Macro-F1 scores suggest reliance on statistical shortcuts.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no numerical performance scores, and public release of the code and dataset is still planned.
infographic.paper_title: OmniTongue: A Comprehensive MLLM Benchmark for Automated Tongue Diagnosis in Traditional Chinese Medicine

title: Toward a digital twin of the ICU patient: Forecasting and treatment response in a generative event model
authors: Zhuoyang Lyu, Yiming Li, Peter C. Hou, Pengyu Hong, Li Zhou
abstract: A digital twin of a patient in intensive care would forecast the patient's course and what a treatment would change. Generative event models, trained to continue a patient's electronic health record (EHR), have been proposed as a path toward such twins. We trained TWICE, a 79M-parameter decoder-only transformer, on the ICU records of one academic health system (127,332 training patients and 1.57 billion tokens). We evaluated it on clinical prediction tasks, generation fidelity, individual trajectories and counterfactual validation. Reading 19 clinical outcomes off 50 simulated futures, with no task-specific training, TWICE matched the best of 144 supervised configurations on held-out patients (mean AUROC 0.836 vs. 0.834). It led on events that change care within a day and trailed on death. With the training data fixed, more and longer simulated futures were worth more than a 6.8-fold larger model. Its generated records matched real ones closely and were as specific to each patient as its own variability allowed. Its predicted risk rose as events approached. Pre-specified controls showed that it reproduced the side effects of drugs and was barely moved by an inert drug. On the values that treatments are given to correct, however, an opposite treatment moved its forecasts like the right one. TWICE forecasts ICU events about as well as task-specific models, and we see it as a step toward a digital twin of the ICU patient.

infographic.key_insight: TWICE forecast ICU outcomes comparably to task-specific models, but its treatment-response forecasts did not reliably distinguish corrective from opposite treatments.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Generative EHR models could support patient-specific ICU forecasting, but these findings do not establish reliable treatment guidance.
method: Trained a 79M-parameter decoder-only transformer to continue ICU electronic health records.
Estimated 19 outcome risks from 50 simulated futures without task-specific training.
Evaluated record fidelity, patient trajectories and counterfactual treatment responses.
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained on 127,332 patients and 1.57 billion tokens from one academic health system, TWICE achieved mean held-out AUROC 0.836 versus 0.834 for the best of 144 supervised configurations.
infographic.watch_item: Opposite treatments shifted forecasts similarly to corrective treatments on targeted clinical values, limiting confidence in causal treatment-response simulation.
infographic.paper_title: Toward a digital twin of the ICU patient: Forecasting and treatment response in a generative event model

title: TabBioMed: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Biomedical Tabular Learning
authors: Pau Mateo-Bernadó, Saivenkata Nagavyjayanthi Polapragada, David Bonet, Pol Arbiol Rakuljic, Laia Mogas Pladevall, Marçal Comajoan Cara
abstract: Recent advances in machine learning have accelerated biomedical prediction, but evaluation on structured biomedical data remains fragmented, especially for datasets with high dimensionality, large sample size, missingness, and class imbalance. We introduce TabBioMed, a large-scale benchmark of 94 curated public biomedical tabular datasets spanning electronic health records, drug discovery, genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, single-cell omics, and systems biology. TabBioMed unifies these datasets through a standardized, dataset-aware preprocessing and evaluation framework, enabling reproducible comparison across classification, regression, and multi-target tasks. We benchmark 23 models across classical baselines, gradient-boosted trees, neural tabular architectures, and tabular foundation models. Foundation models deliver the strongest family-level predictive performance. However, their gains are regime-dependent: tree-based models and tuned multilayer perceptrons remain highly competitive, often dominating under inference-time or training-cost constraints. Overall, TabBioMed shows that biomedical tabular learning is strongly context-dependent, with optimal model choice depending on data regime, task type, and computational budget. We release TabBioMed with curated datasets and splits, preprocessing code, baselines, and results, providing a reproducible benchmark for practical model selection and future methods development in biomedical machine learning, available at https://github.com/AI-sandbox/TabBioMed.

infographic.key_insight: Tabular foundation models perform best overall, but tree-based models and tuned multilayer perceptrons remain competitive depending on the task, data regime, and compute budget.
infographic.clinical_relevance: TabBioMed supports reproducible model comparison for biomedical prediction research, but does not establish readiness for clinical deployment.
method: Curated 94 public biomedical tabular datasets across health records, drug discovery, and omics.
Standardized dataset-aware preprocessing and evaluation for classification, regression, and multi-target tasks.
Benchmarked 23 models spanning classical baselines, boosted trees, neural architectures, and tabular foundation models.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 94 datasets and 23 models, foundation models led at the model-family level, while rankings varied with data regime and computational constraints.
infographic.watch_item: Aggregate benchmark performance does not guarantee the best model for a specific clinical setting; task-specific validation and cost assessment remain necessary.
infographic.paper_title: TabBioMed: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Biomedical Tabular Learning

title: Leakage-Free Is Not Confounder-Free: What a Patient-Level Split Cannot Certify About a Medical Imaging Benchmark
authors: Ignazio Gallo, Mattia Gatti, Leonardo Sgroi, Darwin Castillo, Yuliana Jiménez-Gaona, Nicola Landro
abstract: Patient-level splitting is the standard safeguard against subject leakage in medical imaging evaluation, but it cannot remove a confounder that every fold inherits: an acquisition variable aligned with the diagnosis across the whole cohort. We present a five-question audit of a candidate confounder: how well it predicts the diagnosis, whether it can be decoded from the images, whether diagnostic scores depend on it, whether the image adds predictive value beyond it and how much discrimination survives once it is controlled. We apply it to DMR-IR, the public dataset on which most machine-learning results in breast thermography rest. On 236 patients under a strict patient-disjoint protocol, the acquisition date alone predicts malignancy at AUROC 0.980, above the best of nine imaging arms (0.949), because benign and malignant patients were recruited in different years. The acquisition year is decodable from the pixels among patients who share a diagnosis, largely through a global thermal offset outside the breast, yet only one arm, the one pooling every frame of a visit, demonstrably carries it into its diagnostic score. No arm improves on the date on paired folds, and once the date is controlled, discrimination either collapses or survives only on comparisons the benchmark cannot attribute. The dataset contains only eight cross-label same-date pairs, from ten patients, which limits reliable evaluation within recorded acquisition-date groups. A second, independently acquired cohort, whose dominant channel is patient age, returns the same audit outcome from a different confounder. Mitigation may suppress such a confounder, but without cross-label acquisition support no evaluation on the benchmark can certify that what remains is pathology.

infographic.key_insight: Patient-level splits prevent subject leakage but cannot rule out acquisition-related confounding that may drive apparent diagnostic performance.
infographic.clinical_relevance: High breast thermography benchmark performance may reflect when patients were scanned rather than pathology, limiting its value as evidence for clinical use.
method: Audit five questions covering confounder predictiveness, image decodability, score dependence, added image value and discrimination after control.
Evaluate acquisition-date confounding across nine imaging arms using patient-disjoint splits.
Repeat the audit in an independently acquired cohort with age as the dominant confounding channel.
infographic.evidence_signal: In 236 DMR-IR patients, acquisition date alone achieved AUROC 0.980 versus 0.949 for the best imaging arm; no arm improved on date in paired-fold comparisons.
infographic.watch_item: Only eight cross-label same-date pairs from ten patients limit evaluation within acquisition-date groups, so confounder mitigation alone cannot establish that remaining discrimination reflects pathology.
infographic.paper_title: Leakage-Free Is Not Confounder-Free: What a Patient-Level Split Cannot Certify About a Medical Imaging Benchmark

title: Patient, carer and clinical stakeholder views on using artificial intelligence and machine learning for the histopathological diagnosis of duodenal biopsies
authors: Baby, J. G.; Jaeckle, F.; Williams, J.; Shepherd, K.; Urwin, H.; Soilleux, E. J.
abstract: ObjectiveBiopsies are examined under the microscope by a pathologist, giving a diagnosis, which guides treatment and predicts prognosis. A shortage of pathologists and increasing workload leads to diagnostic delays, while for duodenal (small intestinal) biopsies, variable diagnostic concordance between pathologists limits accuracy. These challenges have motivated us to develop an artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated approach for the automated diagnosis of up to 80% of duodenal biopsies (i.e., most cases of the two most frequent diagnoses: coeliac disease and "normal"). We set out to understand patient, carer and stakeholder views regarding the adoption of such technology. Methods and AnalysisWe conducted mixed-methods stakeholder engagement (February 2024 to June 2026). We ran a national online patients and carers questionnaire (n=231 respondents) and four UK focus-group workshops, one of which additionally captured Likert-scale attitudes1 immediately before and after a structured educational session (n=34 matched pairs). Healthcare professionals completed an online questionnaire (n=37) and took part in a structured workshop. Quantitative data were summarised descriptively; free-text and workshop data were analysed thematically and triangulated across all sources. ResultsMost patients and carers supported AI-reliant diagnosis (68.4%) and would strongly trust systems with formal regulatory approval (66.7%). Most wanted to be informed if AI was used (73.6%), but only 52.4% felt explicit permission was necessary. Qualitative themes centred on clear and available evidence of accuracy, human oversight, transparent communication and clear terminology, with the term machine learning being preferred to artificial intelligence. Agreement ( agree or strongly agree combined) with statements relating to trust, acceptance and perceived benefit of AI was significantly higher after a structured educational session (38.2% to 67.6%, 85.3% to 97.1%, and 52.9% to 97.1% respectively; all p[≤]0.003). Healthcare professionals favoured an AI assistant model over full automation, citing the need for validation, explainability, data governance and workflow integration. Patients also preferred some level of human oversight. ConclusionPatients and healthcare professionals are cautiously supportive of AI-assisted diagnosis of duodenal biopsies, conditional upon demonstration of accuracy, appropriate human oversight and transparent communication. Attitudes towards AI-assisted diagnosis were more favourable after structured explanation. Key MessagesO_ST_ABSWhat is already known on this topicC_ST_ABSVery little is known about patients, carers or healthcare professionals views about the automation of diagnosis in pathology, using AI-based software solutions. What this study adds{Rightarrow} This is the first study to investigate patient, carer and healthcare professional attitudes specifically to AI-mediated duodenal biopsy diagnosis. Around two-thirds of respondents supported AI-assisted diagnosis, contingent upon clear and available evidence of accuracy, appropriate human oversight and transparent communication, together with appropriate regulatory approval of the technology. {Rightarrow}Attitudes were markedly more favourable after a single structured educational session: agreement that AI could improve duodenal biopsy diagnosis nearly doubled and trust in healthcare AI rose substantially, suggesting that public views of AI in diagnosis can be influenced by clear explanation. {Rightarrow}Patients and healthcare professionals both favour some ongoing level of human oversight of any AI-based diagnostic approach. How this study might affect research, practice or policy{Rightarrow} Our study suggests that a phased, AI-assistant-first deployment model with defined validation and audit checkpoints would be most readily acceptable when introducing diagnostic AI into histopathology. {Rightarrow}It indicates that appropriate information and education, for example, a patient and public involvement and engagement (PPIE) session, can increase trust in AI in healthcare. {Rightarrow}It shows that patients and the public are more trusting of technology for which the term machine learning is used, rather than artificial intelligence (AI). {Rightarrow}It offers a stakeholder-engagement template for use by others introducing AI-based diagnostics.

infographic.key_insight: Most surveyed patients and carers supported AI-based duodenal biopsy diagnosis, while stakeholders emphasised accuracy evidence, human oversight and transparency.
infographic.clinical_relevance: AI could help address pathology workload and diagnostic delays, but this study assessed stakeholder views rather than diagnostic performance or patient outcomes.
method: Mixed-methods engagement using questionnaires, workshops and thematic analysis.
Patient/carer survey: 231 respondents; four UK focus-group workshops.
Healthcare professional survey: 37 respondents; education-session attitudes assessed in 34 matched pairs.
infographic.evidence_signal: Patient/carer support was 68.4%; in the 34 matched pairs, agreement on trust rose from 38.2% before education to 67.6% afterward.
infographic.watch_item: Small professional and pre/post samples limit generalisability; clinical adoption still requires validation, governance and workflow integration.
infographic.paper_title: Patient, carer and clinical stakeholder views on using artificial intelligence and machine learning for the histopathological diagnosis of duodenal biopsies

title: MedicalRSI: Medical Recursive Self-Improving Agents via Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution
authors: Ziqing Wang, Hamid Palangi, Lili Zhao, Kaize Ding
abstract: Medical agents built on large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet most stay fixed once deployed and do not keep using their experience to improve later attempts. As a result, the same kind of error can recur across patients. To address this, existing self-improvement methods update an agent's weights or its medical harness from its own experience, but their improving strategy stays fixed and never learns which changes actually help, which caps how much the agent can improve. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) instead improves both the agent and its improving strategy. However, achieving RSI for medical agents is challenging, because clinical workflows rarely come with a reference harness, and a change that fixes early errors may not fix the problems the agent meets later. We propose MedicalRSI, an RSI framework built on Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution, in which one model plays two roles. The Solver is the medical agent itself, and the Improver is its learnable improving strategy, which writes a medical harness from the agent's failures. Each harness is rewarded by its gain over acting without it, and both roles are trained together, so the Improver keeps adapting to the problems the Solver has not yet solved. On multiple benchmarks and LLM backbones, MedicalRSI outperforms existing context-level and weight-level self-improvement methods and transfers well to unseen workflows, new LLMs and new databases, a step toward medical agents that keep improving.

infographic.key_insight: MedicalRSI jointly improves a medical AI agent and its strategy for learning from failures, rather than keeping that improvement strategy fixed.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could help medical AI adapt to recurring errors and unfamiliar workflows, but clinical benefit and safety remain unestablished.
method: One model serves as both Solver and Improver.
The Improver writes a medical harness from Solver failures and is rewarded for gains over performance without it.
Both roles train together so the improvement strategy adapts to the Solver’s remaining weaknesses.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports gains over context- and weight-level self-improvement methods across multiple benchmarks and LLM backbones, plus transfer to unseen workflows, models, and databases; no numerical results are provided.
infographic.watch_item: Continual updates would require safety validation and monitoring before clinical deployment.
infographic.paper_title: MedicalRSI: Medical Recursive Self-Improving Agents via Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution

title: Beyond Final Answers: Interpretable Tumor Immune Microenvironment Reasoning from H&E and mIF
authors: Yixuan Duan, Kexin Geng, Hanwen Xu, Wei Qiu
abstract: Readouts of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), such as CD8+ T-cell density, intra-epithelial infiltration and the Ki67 index, combine tissue architecture from H&E with cell phenotypes from multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF). Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) could automate these readouts with an explanation, but two gaps remain. Pathology MLLMs read H&E alone, while these readouts need the cell phenotypes that mIF measures. And their reasoning has no step-level truth to be checked against, so R1-style reinforcement learning rewards only the final answer and leaves the reasoning unverified. Same-section H&E and mIF provide what both gaps lack: mIF measures every cell without manual annotation, which gives cell-level ground truth for each step that clinical guidelines prescribe, from delineating a tissue compartment to counting and normalizing the marker-positive cells within it. We therefore present HERMES (H&E-mIF Reasoning with Multimodal Evidence Supervision), an R1-style MLLM that reasons jointly over paired H&E and mIF in guideline steps and is trained with a process reward that checks every stated quantity against this truth. Across four field-level TIME tasks in colorectal cancer, HERMES (4B) reaches an average accuracy of 84.5%, compared with 74.7% for the strongest of twelve proprietary, general, medical and pathology MLLMs, and a higher share of its intermediate quantities is correct than for the strongest open-weight baseline. Without the process reward, reinforcement learning barely improves on supervised fine-tuning (80.0% vs. 78.8%) and fewer stated quantities are correct; editing a decisive stated quantity changes the answer as implied in all 885 test questions. Without retraining, it keeps the highest average accuracy on an external cohort imaged with CODEX (76.4% vs. 67.3%) and on head and neck cancer, a cancer type absent from training (76.7% vs. 72.5%).

infographic.key_insight: HERMES combines H&E and multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) images with step-level supervision to improve tumor immune microenvironment readouts and make intermediate quantities checkable.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach could support pathology research by linking tissue architecture with immune-cell phenotypes, but clinical utility remains unproven.
method: Reasons jointly over paired, same-section H&E and mIF images.
Uses mIF-derived cell-level measurements to supervise guideline-based reasoning steps.
Applies reinforcement learning rewards that check stated intermediate quantities, not just final answers.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four colorectal cancer tasks, HERMES achieved 84.5% average accuracy versus 74.7% for the strongest comparator, and retained an accuracy lead without retraining on external CODEX and head-and-neck cancer evaluations.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment would require reliable paired-image alignment and phenotype measurements, plus validation beyond the reported field-level research tasks.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond Final Answers: Interpretable Tumor Immune Microenvironment Reasoning from H&E and mIF

title: Learning 3D MRI Representations with Generative Adversarial Networks
authors: Sujeet Lahane, Sapna Mishra, Akash Suryavanshi, Tapan Gandhi, Bharat Biswal
abstract: Learning representations of visual images is a challenging task. It requires extracting abstract patterns from high-dimensional data without explicit supervision. This becomes pronounced with 3D MR imaging due to sparse features, higher dimensional inputs, and smaller datasets. Many state-of-the-art representation learning algorithms successfully rely on transformers and diffusion-based architectures. However, these methods struggle with smaller datasets. In effect, solution methods relax the problem by slicing 3D volumes and solving the problem for 2D medical imaging, resulting in a loss of spatial 3D information. We present R2RG, a representation learning method based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) honing the reconstruction task. Our key insights lie in exploiting architectural biases in 3D CNNs, combined with data-efficient auto-encoding GANs and a composite loss function to enhance reconstruction fidelity and stabilize training. Our experiments on three standard datasets and a locally collected dataset show that R2RG not only achieves superior performance but also generalizes to heterogeneous and smaller datasets. Furthermore, representations learned with R2RG outperform those learned with contrastive-based representation learning methods on Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease classification. Our work demonstrates that reconstruction-based representation learning is a promising direction for 3D medical imaging under limited data availability.

infographic.key_insight: R2RG learns 3D MRI representations through GAN-enhanced reconstruction, preserving volumetric information while targeting limited-data settings.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The learned representations may support Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease classification research, but clinical utility is not established by the abstract.
method: Uses 3D CNNs to retain spatial information across MRI volumes.
Combines auto-encoding with GAN-based reconstruction refinement.
Applies a composite loss to improve reconstruction fidelity and stabilize training.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three standard datasets and one locally collected dataset, the authors report generalization to smaller, heterogeneous datasets and better disease classification than contrastive-learning representations.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no dataset sizes, numerical effect estimates, or clinical validation details, limiting assessment of robustness and deployment readiness.
infographic.paper_title: Learning 3D MRI Representations with Generative Adversarial Networks

title: Multi-Tier Edge Triage: Optimizing Latency for Safe Clinical Agents
authors: Joshua Broyde, Sarita A. Joshi
abstract: Deploying generative AI agents in enterprise clinical workflows requires enforcing multi-dimensional safety and compliance policies--preventing HIPAA Protected Health Information (PHI) exposure, maintaining clinical scope-of-practice boundaries, ensuring patient-appropriate reading comprehension, and preserving brand integrity--under interactive latency constraints. Synchronous outbound calls to cloud Large Language Model (LLM) judges add substantial network and decoding overhead onto the critical response path. We present Multi-Tier Edge Triage, a safety screening architecture that co-locates a compact Tier-1 sequence classifier on the clinical agent's host server, resolving clear queries in-process without a network round-trip and escalating only ambiguous queries to a Tier-2 cloud LLM judge. To evaluate Tier-1 encoders without length or unigram shortcuts, we construct four length-matched contrastive twin benchmarks seeded from MedSafetyBench, ASQ-PHI, and a synthetic four-mandate clinical assistant policy (Generic HealthCorp). While frozen local encoders match cloud models on structured PHI detection (>= 98.3% accuracy in <= 23.5 ms), they degrade markedly on semantic safety and symmetric-blocklist prompts. However, end-to-end representation fine-tuning closes the multi-policy accuracy gap: a fine-tuned 335M-parameter BGE-Large classifier achieves 98.90% out-of-fold accuracy versus 99.20% for a zero-shot cloud LLM judge (exact McNemar p = 0.648, zero shared errors), 97.8%-98.2% recall, and a 0.0%-0.4% over-refusal rate in 39.0 ms (>14x faster than cloud LLM evaluation on our benchmark host). Per-policy error analysis reveals ceiling local recall on PHI (100.0%), brand (100.0%), and clinical scope (98.7%-99.3%) violations, isolating residual errors to reading-level checks (93.3%-95.3%) and motivating targeted multi-tier escalation.

infographic.key_insight: A fine-tuned local safety classifier approached cloud-judge accuracy while screening in 39.0 ms, supporting rapid triage with cloud escalation for ambiguous cases.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Local screening could reduce safety-check delays in clinical AI workflows while checking PHI exposure, clinical scope, reading level, and brand-policy compliance.
method: Screen queries with an on-host Tier-1 classifier; escalate ambiguous cases to a Tier-2 cloud LLM judge.
Evaluate four length-matched contrastive twin benchmarks designed to limit length and unigram shortcuts.
Fine-tune a 335M-parameter BGE-Large encoder for multi-policy classification.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the multi-policy benchmark, the fine-tuned classifier achieved 98.90% out-of-fold accuracy versus 99.20% for a zero-shot cloud judge (exact McNemar p = 0.648), with over 14× faster evaluation on the benchmark host.
infographic.watch_item: Reading-level violation recall remained lower at 93.3%–95.3%; benchmark results do not establish real-world clinical safety or validate escalation thresholds.
infographic.paper_title: Multi-Tier Edge Triage: Optimizing Latency for Safe Clinical Agents

title: Neurodegenerative Differential Diagnosis with Knowledge-enhanced Structural Reasoning
authors: Mingxuan Wang, Siyuan Du, Yanfeng Wang, Ya Zhang, Chencheng Zhang, Jiangchao Yao
abstract: Accurate differential diagnosis of neurodegenerative disorders remains challenging due to overlapping clinical manifestations and heterogeneous, often incomplete multimodal observations. Existing multimodal models can integrate imaging and clinical measurements but often overlook disease-specific evidence patterns and pairwise relations among competing diagnoses. We therefore propose Knowledge-enhanced Structural Reasoning (KnowSR), which aligns multimodal patient representations with a literature-grounded knowledge bank of disease prototypes, signed evidence directions, and pairwise diagnostic relations. Specifically, in KnowSR, patient-specific knowledge alignment and target-aware pooling inject structured disease evidence, while anchored relational reasoning reconciles pairwise diagnostic margins over a sparse differential graph, thereby collectively enhancing differential diagnostic capability. Across extensive experiments, KnowSR consistently outperforms 19 baselines on patient-level six-class diagnosis under patient-disjoint five-fold evaluation. This shows that grounding patient evidence in structured medical knowledge enables more effective differential diagnosis than naive multimodal fusion alone.

infographic.key_insight: KnowSR combines multimodal patient data with structured disease knowledge to better distinguish neurodegenerative disorders with overlapping features.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support differential diagnosis when imaging and clinical observations overlap or are incomplete, but clinical utility remains unestablished.
method: Aligns patient representations with literature-grounded disease prototypes and evidence directions.
Uses target-aware pooling to incorporate disease-specific evidence.
Reconciles pairwise diagnostic comparisons over a sparse graph of competing diagnoses.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent gains over 19 baselines for patient-level six-class diagnosis using patient-disjoint five-fold evaluation, without numerical results or dataset sizes.
infographic.watch_item: External validation is not described in the abstract, leaving generalizability to other clinical settings uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Neurodegenerative Differential Diagnosis with Knowledge-enhanced Structural Reasoning

title: Scalable Evaluation of Medical AI using Evidence-based Practice Recommendations
authors: Teya Bergamaschi, Bijal Rajput, Akshay Goel, Matthew Thompson, Jacqueline Shreibati, Dave Steiner
abstract: Rigorously evaluating medical artificial intelligence (AI) requires testing open-ended clinical management across diverse presentations and stages of care. However, existing benchmarks rely on manual expert authoring, limiting coverage across conditions, conditional care pathways, and evolving guidelines. We develop an automated pipeline that extracts and verifies structured clinical criteria and branching decision trees from practice recommendations to generate scenarios spanning the care continuum, including nuanced presentations and practice variations across regions and guideline editions. Applied to 436 BMJ Best Practice clinical monographs (354 US, 82 International), this yields 3,200 scenarios spanning differential diagnosis, investigations, treatment, and complications, plus targeted suites for regional specificity (731 US/International pairs) and temporal freshness (630 scenarios). To grade responses, we develop a clinician-calibrated autorater that scores management plans on a 4-point rubric stratifying deviations by clinical severity. Across Gemini models, scaling improves adherence, while web search (+0.8 percentage points [pp] on average) and multi-sample synthesis (+2.2 pp) combine additively (+2.8 pp). In context, full monographs consistently trail condensed excerpts. On targeted suites, web search narrows international performance gaps (+4.2 pp) and improves adherence to newly updated guidance (+4.6 pp). In a study with Primary Care Physicians (n = 9) across 200 scenarios, AI assistance raises adherence from 50.5% to 70.0%, driven largely by fewer clinical omissions. Overall, our results demonstrate a scalable evaluation setup using an evidence-based corpus originally written to guide human clinical decision-making, and demonstrate its viability to assess medical AI and its assistance on clinician decision-making.

infographic.key_insight: An automated, guideline-based evaluation pipeline enables broad testing of medical AI, while a small physician study found higher guideline adherence with AI assistance.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could help assess whether AI-generated management plans follow evidence-based recommendations across care stages, regions, and guideline updates.
method: Extract and verify clinical criteria and branching decision trees from practice recommendations.
Generate scenarios covering diagnosis, investigations, treatment, and complications.
Grade management plans with a clinician-calibrated autorater using a 4-point, severity-based rubric.
infographic.evidence_signal: From 436 BMJ Best Practice monographs, researchers generated 3,200 core scenarios; in 200 scenarios evaluated by 9 primary care physicians, AI assistance increased adherence from 50.5% to 70.0%.
infographic.watch_item: Guideline adherence in scenario-based testing does not establish improved patient outcomes, and the physician study was small.
infographic.paper_title: Scalable Evaluation of Medical AI using Evidence-based Practice Recommendations

title: LesionAgent: Training-Free Agentic Tumor Tracking and Response Assessment in Longitudinal CT
authors: Maximilian Rokuss, Jeya Maria Jose Valanarasu, Alejandro Lozano, Benjamin Hamm, Yannick Kirchhoff, Fabian Isensee
abstract: Every few months, a cancer patient's CT scans decide whether treatment continues. 3D foundation models can now detect, segment, register and track lesions, yet none of them reads the scans as a radiologist does. A radiologist decides which findings are lesions, which are the same lesion months later and whether a new spot means progression, and checks each decision against the extensive rules of a clinical guideline. We introduce LesionAgent, an LLM agent that performs this read end to end without task-specific training. It operates frozen 3D models as tools, acts in 3D through coordinate-labelled views, remembers every lesion across visits in a registry, verifies every model output it relies on, and leaves every number to a deterministic guideline engine. On four public longitudinal CT datasets, LesionAgent tracks more lesions and measures them more accurately than every automatic baseline, and where the same 3D models chained by fixed rules call progression falsely at 33 of 56 follow-ups, it does so twice. On clinical follow-up CTs, it agrees with the radiologists' response at 20 of 23 follow-ups, including every change in response, and without training on DeepLesion, it retrieves more of its lesions than every tracker trained on it (89.0% vs. 87.4%). Its harness, not its LLM, makes the difference: given the same LLM and 3D models but not the harness, Claude Code reaches a detection F1 of 41% and LesionAgent 78%, and an open-weight LLM that can run inside the hospital rises from 6% to 73%. LesionAgent and a napari reading app for any LLM are available at https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/LesionAgent.

infographic.key_insight: LesionAgent pairs an LLM with frozen 3D imaging tools and a structured workflow to track tumors across CT scans without task-specific training.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support more consistent longitudinal tumor assessment by linking lesions across visits and applying response guidelines deterministically.
method: Uses frozen 3D models through coordinate-labelled views.
Maintains a cross-visit lesion registry and verifies model outputs.
Delegates numerical response assessment to a deterministic guideline engine.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four public longitudinal CT datasets, LesionAgent outperformed automatic baselines; it falsely called progression at 2 of 56 follow-ups versus 33 for a fixed-rule pipeline and matched radiologists’ response assessments at 20 of 23 clinical follow-ups.
infographic.watch_item: The small clinical evaluation leaves generalizability and prospective workflow safety unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: LesionAgent: Training-Free Agentic Tumor Tracking and Response Assessment in Longitudinal CT

title: A Neurosymbolic Multimodal Framework for 30-Day Diabetic Readmission Prediction: Integrating Structured EHR Data, Dense Clinical Embeddings, and Knowledge-Grounded Symbolic Extraction
authors: Una Suman Kumar Patro, Sibangi Subhadarsani, Narendra Badam
abstract: Unplanned 30-day readmissions among patients with diabetes mellitus impose a substantial clinical and economic burden, yet most predictive models use only structured electronic health record (EHR) data and ignore free-text clinical notes, which often contain code-mixed Hindi-English (Hinglish) phrasing and negation that general-purpose language models parse unreliably. We propose a neurosymbolic multimodal framework evaluated on the public Diabetes 130-US Hospitals dataset (101,766 encounters; 71,518 patients) with a patient-level grouped 80/20 split. Three streams are fused: engineered structured features; 32 components of Bio_ClinicalBERT note embeddings obtained by truncated singular value decomposition; and symbolic entities extracted by an open-weight clinical language model within a three-stage hybrid retrieval-augmented generation pipeline (dense retrieval, sparse lexical retrieval, and cross-encoder re-ranking) with reflective negation auditing. A cost-sensitive XGBoost classifier with a decision threshold calibrated by Youden's J statistic produces the prediction. On the held-out test cohort (n = 20,153), the structured baseline achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.6477, sensitivity of 0.5839, and Brier score of 0.1080. The full multimodal model achieved the highest sensitivity (0.6667; +8.28 percentage points), the best F2-score (0.3824), and the lowest Brier score (0.0977), at a slightly lower AUROC (0.6375) and specificity (0.5161). Shapley additive explanations showed that prior utilization dominates risk, with compressed narrative components among the top predictors. On a 500-note code-switched benchmark, grounded retrieval raised Hinglish symptom recall from 4.8% to 40.2% and precision from 3.1% to 45.2%, while reducing entity hallucinations from 1.74 to 0.00 per note.

infographic.key_insight: Combining structured EHR features, clinical-text embeddings, and knowledge-grounded entity extraction improved sensitivity for 30-day diabetic readmission prediction, but slightly reduced AUROC.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework could help identify more patients who are later readmitted, although low specificity may increase false-positive alerts.
method: Fuse engineered EHR features with 32 compressed Bio_ClinicalBERT embedding components.
Extract symbolic entities using hybrid retrieval, cross-encoder re-ranking, and reflective negation auditing.
Predict readmission with cost-sensitive XGBoost and a threshold calibrated using Youden’s J.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using a patient-grouped 80/20 split of 101,766 encounters, the model achieved sensitivity of 0.6667 versus 0.5839 and Brier score of 0.0977 versus 0.1080 on 20,153 held-out encounters; AUROC fell from 0.6477 to 0.6375.
infographic.watch_item: Prospective clinical utility remains unestablished; specificity of 0.5161 warrants careful assessment of false-positive burden before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: A Neurosymbolic Multimodal Framework for 30-Day Diabetic Readmission Prediction: Integrating Structured EHR Data, Dense Clinical Embeddings, and Knowledge-Grounded Symbolic Extraction

title: Adversarial Robustness of Capsule Networks for Medical Image Classification
authors: Srinivasan, A.; Sritharan, D. V.; Chadha, S.; Fu, D.; Hossain, J. O.; Breuer, G. A.; Aneja, S.
abstract: PurposeDeep learning models are increasingly being used in medical diagnostics, but their vulnerability to adversarial perturbations raises concerns about their reliability in clinical applications. Capsule networks (CapsNets) are a promising architecture for medical imaging tasks, given their ability to model spatial relationships and train with smaller amounts of data. Although previous studies have focused on adversarial training approaches to improve robustness, exploring alternative architectures is an underexplored direction for combating poor adversarial stability. Prior work has suggested that CapsNets may exhibit improved robustness to adversarial perturbations compared to convolutional neural networks (CNNs), but performance on adversarial images has not been studied systematically in clinical environments. We evaluated the robustness of CapsNets compared to CNNs and vision transformers (ViTs) across multiple medical image classification tasks. MethodsWe trained two CNNs (ResNet-18 and ResNet-50), one ViT (MedViT), and two CapsNets (DR-CapsNet and BP-CapsNet) on four distinct medical imaging datasets (PneumoniaMNIST, BreastMNIST, NoduleMNIST3D, and BloodMNIST) and one natural image dataset (MNIST). Models were evaluated on adversarial examples generated by projected gradient descent, fast gradient sign method, AutoAttack, Carlini & Wagner, and black-box transfer attacks. Models also underwent PGD adversarial fine-tuning to assess whether architectural differences persisted after adversarial training. Interpretability experiments, including latent space and Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) analyses, were conducted to better understand model stability on adversarial inputs. ResultsUnder conventional training, CapsNets demonstrated superior robustness under adversarial perturbations compared to CNNs and ViTs across all medical imaging datasets and the natural image dataset. Latent space and Grad-CAM visualizations revealed that CapsNets maintained more consistent feature representations and attention maps after adversarial perturbations compared to CNNs and ViTs, suggesting that advantages in CapsNet robustness are supported, at least in part, by more stable feature encodings. PGD adversarial fine-tuning improved robustness across models, with MedViT exhibiting the largest gains and thereby narrowing the performance gap. ConclusionCapsNets exhibit advantages in adversarial robustness over CNN- and ViT-based models on medical imaging tasks. These findings suggest that capsule-based architectures may be a promising direction for robust medical image classification. Future work should validate CapsNet robustness across more complex medical imaging tasks, independent external datasets, and broader sources of real-world imaging variability.

infographic.key_insight: Under conventional training, capsule networks showed greater adversarial robustness than the tested CNNs and vision transformer across five image datasets.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Capsule networks may help improve medical imaging model reliability under adversarial perturbations, but clinical safety and effectiveness remain unestablished.
method: Compared two capsule networks, ResNet-18, ResNet-50, and MedViT.
Evaluated five adversarial attack approaches and performed PGD adversarial fine-tuning.
Analyzed latent representations and Grad-CAM maps to explore model stability.
infographic.evidence_signal: Testing covered four medical imaging datasets and MNIST; the abstract reports more stable capsule-network representations and attention maps under adversarial perturbations.
infographic.watch_item: The supplied abstract is incomplete and provides no numerical effect sizes or post-fine-tuning results, limiting assessment of the robustness advantage.
infographic.paper_title: Adversarial Robustness of Capsule Networks for Medical Image Classification

title: Communication-Efficient Federated Learning of Latent Patient Representations from Multi-Institutional EHRs
authors: Zhiyu Yan, Shiao Liu, Rahul Mahajan, Anand Viswanathan, Christopher D. Anderson, Rui Duan
abstract: Electronic health records (EHRs) contain rich health information for uncovering latent patient representations and clinically meaningful subgroups. Learning from EHR data across institutions is valuable because representations learned at a single site may reflect local data patterns and lack generalizability, yet pooling patient-level records across institutions is often impractical because of privacy constraints and communication costs. We propose a communication-efficient, non-iterative federated spectral method for learning shared latent representation components from multi-institutional EHRs, in which each institution shares aggregate marginal frequencies and a low-rank spectral summary while keeping patient-level records local. A central server aggregates these summaries with the pooled marginal frequencies to recover both the shared low-rank structure and the canonical row-normalization direction required for interpretable representation recovery. We prove row-wise recovery guarantees and error bounds, with a leading federated variance term matching a corresponding lower bound under explicit regularity conditions. Simulations show that our method closely matches pooled analysis in estimating latent representation components, improves as more sites contribute summaries, and outperforms single-site and existing federated benchmarks across a range of data settings. Applied to real-world multi-facility EHR data for stroke patients, the method learns interpretable patient representations that highlight clinically distinct subgroups and could help inform subgroup-specific care.

infographic.key_insight: A non-iterative federated spectral method learns shared latent patient representations across institutions without pooling patient-level EHR records.
infographic.clinical_relevance: In stroke EHR data, the learned representations highlight clinically distinct patient subgroups, though benefits for care decisions remain untested.
method: Each institution shares aggregate marginal frequencies and a low-rank spectral summary while retaining patient-level records locally.
A central server combines summaries to recover shared representation components and their normalization.
Theoretical analysis provides row-wise recovery guarantees and error bounds under explicit regularity conditions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations closely matched pooled analysis and outperformed single-site and existing federated benchmarks; multi-facility stroke EHR data demonstrated interpretable subgroups.
infographic.watch_item: Keeping records local does not by itself guarantee privacy; shared summaries require disclosure-risk assessment.
infographic.paper_title: Communication-Efficient Federated Learning of Latent Patient Representations from Multi-Institutional EHRs

title: From Sequence Uncertainty to Phenotype Hypotheses: Uncertainty-Conditioned Inference over Biomedical Knowledge Graphs
authors: Huixin Zhan, Jason H. Moore
abstract: Genomic foundation models provide variant-level evidence, but connecting that evidence to phenotype hypotheses requires accounting for uncertainty throughout structured reasoning. We introduce an uncertainty-conditioned path-energy framework that converts sequence predictions and calibrated predictive uncertainty into explicit distributions over graph-supported phenotype hypotheses, without patient-level phenotype supervision. An interpretable learned energy scores admissible gene--disease--phenotype routes, query uncertainty controls the target temperature, and path probabilities are aggregated into phenotype hypotheses. This formulation makes evidence quality an explicit determinant of hypothesis breadth while retaining traceable multi-path support. Exact normalization over enumerable candidate sets provides a reference for evaluating a Hastings-corrected learned revision operator. On AlzKB and Hetionet, phenotype-level entropy tracks upstream uncertainty, with Spearman correlations of 0.951 and 0.878, respectively; ablations identify the contribution of uncertainty conditioning. In masked-edge recovery, the model exceeds chance and degree-matched probability-permutation controls. Training the energy under the uncertainty-dependent temperature yields higher held-out recall@10 than training under a constant temperature of comparable magnitude. Under gene hold-out, recall@10 exceeds that of a trained DistMult embedding on 24 of 30 graph masks (0.183 versus 0.123); this difference is attributable mainly to three genes with many variants and is not established for all genes. These results establish an uncertainty-aware interface from genomic predictions to graph-supported phenotype hypotheses that combines interpretable probability allocation with held-out association recovery of explicitly stated scope.

infographic.key_insight: An uncertainty-conditioned framework turns genomic model predictions into traceable, graph-supported phenotype hypotheses, with upstream uncertainty shaping hypothesis breadth.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support research prioritization of phenotype hypotheses from genomic evidence, but clinical utility is not established.
method: Score admissible gene–disease–phenotype paths with an interpretable learned energy.
Use calibrated predictive uncertainty to set the temperature of path probabilities.
Aggregate path probabilities into phenotype hypotheses without patient-level phenotype supervision.
infographic.evidence_signal: On AlzKB and Hetionet, phenotype entropy tracked upstream uncertainty (Spearman 0.951 and 0.878); gene-holdout recall@10 exceeded trained DistMult on 24 of 30 graph masks (0.183 vs 0.123).
infographic.watch_item: The gene-holdout advantage was driven mainly by three genes with many variants and is not established across all genes.
infographic.paper_title: From Sequence Uncertainty to Phenotype Hypotheses: Uncertainty-Conditioned Inference over Biomedical Knowledge Graphs

title: DiagTrace: An Interactive Benchmark for Clinical Decision Making
authors: Yufan Wang, Rui Yang, Yi Lin, Chunhua Weng, Yifan Peng
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on medical question answering and diagnostic reasoning benchmarks. However, existing evaluations typically provide all patient information upfront and assess only the final diagnosis or rationale. This setup ignores the need to acquire diagnostic evidence incrementally from incomplete information in real-world diagnosis. To bridge this gap, we introduce DiagTrace, a source-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can reconstruct the documented diagnostic trajectory through interactive information seeking. Each benchmark instance is built from a PubMed Central case report and includes an initial presentation, an event bank, a clinical course, and diagnostic references. DiagTrace contains 510 cases across eight specialties, with 225 used to evaluate four LLMs on clinical-course alignment, interaction quality, and efficiency. Results reveal trade-offs in coverage, source-consistent ordering, and turn use.

infographic.key_insight: DiagTrace evaluates how LLMs seek diagnostic evidence step by step, rather than judging only a final diagnosis from fully supplied patient information.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The benchmark examines information-seeking behavior relevant to clinical reasoning, but does not establish safety or effectiveness in patient care.
method: Build source-grounded cases from PubMed Central case reports.
Provide an initial presentation, event bank, documented clinical course, and diagnostic references.
Assess interactive reconstruction of the documented diagnostic trajectory.
infographic.evidence_signal: DiagTrace contains 510 cases across eight specialties; evaluation of four LLMs on 225 cases revealed trade-offs in coverage, source-consistent ordering, and turn use.
infographic.watch_item: Alignment with a published case trajectory should not be equated with an optimal diagnostic strategy or real-world clinical validity.
infographic.paper_title: DiagTrace: An Interactive Benchmark for Clinical Decision Making

title: Observed, Curated, Reused: Observation Bias in Clinical AI Evaluation
authors: Md Shamim Ahmed, Lukas Galke Poech, Richard Röttger
abstract: Clinical AI evaluations are vulnerable to observation bias embedded in routine medical documentation, which captures only what clinicians notice, test, and record rather than a complete clinical picture. As this evidence travels into publications and reference knowledge graphs, crucial distinctions disappear: unexamined symptoms blur with confirmed negatives, and chronological disease progression is lost. Surviving evidence can also enter both the benchmark query and the reference knowledge base, creating a self-referential loop where a patient is evaluated against clues derived from their own published case report. To quantify this bias, we tracked 6,503 clinical cases across six historical Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) releases (October 2021-June 2026) to identify when HPO first cited the publications describing them. This yielded a confirmatory cohort with an observable "source ingestion" event, where HPO cited a case's source publication as target-disease evidence. Diagnostic rankers depended heavily on these source publications: for our primary semantic ranker (Resnik), publication-weighted mean reciprocal rank rose from 0.26 before paper ingestion to 0.84 upon inclusion in HPO, but collapsed to 0.05 when source-linked assertions were counterfactually removed. Two additional rankers (IC-cosine and LIRICAL) reproduced this trajectory, and control experiments confirmed the diagnostic jump was driven by the patient's publication rather than background HPO growth. Clinical AI systems may therefore score well because their knowledge base contains evidence linked to the test case's source publication, rather than through generalization. Modern knowledge is not the problem; evaluation evidence must match the claim. Trustworthy benchmarks must separate patients, source-linked evidence, and time: historical tests should use only knowledge available at the intended decision time.

infographic.key_insight: Clinical AI diagnostic rankings can appear stronger when the reference knowledge base includes evidence from the test case’s own source publication, rather than reflecting generalization.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Trustworthy diagnostic benchmarks should separate patients, source-linked evidence, and time to avoid overstating performance relevant to clinical use.
method: Tracked 6,503 clinical cases across six HPO releases spanning October 2021–June 2026.
Identified when HPO first cited each case’s source publication as target-disease evidence.
Compared three diagnostic rankers before ingestion, after ingestion, and after removing source-linked assertions.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the confirmatory cohort, Resnik’s publication-weighted mean reciprocal rank rose from 0.26 before source ingestion to 0.84 afterward, then fell to 0.05 when source-linked assertions were removed; two additional rankers showed the same trajectory.
infographic.watch_item: These case-publication-based results flag benchmark contamination but do not establish performance in prospective clinical care.
infographic.paper_title: Observed, Curated, Reused: Observation Bias in Clinical AI Evaluation

title: Towards Text-Mask Consistency in Medical Image Segmentation
authors: Jie Gui, Hang Tu, Wen Sha, Xiuquan Du
abstract: Vision-language models for medical image segmentation often produce masks that conflict with the accompanying text, especially under multi-site/multi-lesion descriptions. We trace this failure to two factors: (i) highly templated and repetitive clinical language causes one-to-one hard contrastive learning to yield numerous false negatives, weakening cross-modal alignment; and (ii) predominantly vision-driven, one-way cross-attention lacks a language-dominant, spatially aware pathway, hindering effective injection of textual semantics into the spatial visual domain. To this end, we propose Consistency-enhanced Two-stage Segmentation (C2Seg). In the pretraining stage, Cluster-aware Contrastive Learning uses a frozen strong baseline to construct an intra-batch text similarity matrix as soft labels, thereby alleviating false negative conflicts and producing more discriminative visual representations. In the fusion stage, we introduce a Bidirectional Complementary Attention Module, where each modality dominates attention along its own path, fostering deep interaction and structural consistency between visual and textual representations. In order to enhance the expressive power of multimodal features, we further adopt KAN-based Attention Gating. Without updating the language encoder, our approach significantly improves text-mask consistency and segmentation accuracy on four public medical imaging datasets. The source code is available at https://github.com/JGuiidev/C2Seg.

infographic.key_insight: C2Seg aims to make medical image segmentation masks better match text descriptions, particularly when multiple sites or lesions are described.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Better text–mask agreement could support more faithful text-guided image analysis, but clinical benefit is not established by the abstract.
method: Cluster-aware contrastive pretraining uses soft text-similarity labels to reduce false-negative conflicts.
Bidirectional complementary attention strengthens spatial interaction between image and text features.
KAN-based attention gating enriches multimodal features while the language encoder remains frozen.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors report improved text–mask consistency and segmentation accuracy on four public medical imaging datasets, without numerical results in the abstract.
infographic.watch_item: Performance on public datasets does not establish reliability across clinical settings; external validation remains important.
infographic.paper_title: Towards Text-Mask Consistency in Medical Image Segmentation
